note: Route not in the reports, drawn approximately. Sailing from Gourock on 1 Nov and arriving at Mers El Kébir on 11 Nov fits convoy KMF 2 (Clyde 1 Nov, North Africa 11–12 Nov 1942). Like the other Torch convoys it is drawn down the Firth of Clyde, through the North Channel, west round Ireland, far out into the Atlantic away from U-boats and aircraft, and east through the Strait of Gibraltar. The exact track isn't known.

Route not in the reports, drawn approximately: out past Sandy Hook, south of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, across the North Atlantic, round the north of Ireland and up the Firth of Clyde to Greenock. The Queen Elizabeth crossed alone, without escort, relying on her speed; she took about five days (sailed 31 Aug 10:05, anchored at Greenock 5 Sep 19:00).

Rail route not in the reports, drawn approximately. They say only that the battery entrained and then boarded lorries; the stops (Glasgow, Carlisle, Crewe, Birmingham, Oxford, Reading, Pewsey) are a guess from the 1940s rail network, and the line from Greenock to Glasgow is not traced. The reported times (entrained 0230, arrived 0330) are too short for about 400 miles and were probably typed loosely. The route runs well to the west of London. The train (inferred; the reports don't describe it): a British troop special of compartment coaches, the British passenger car being "designed to effect ready discharge of passengers from many compartments" (Bykofsky and Larson, The Transportation Corps: Operations Overseas, 1957, p. 122). From the Clyde it ran on the LMS (Gourock and Greenock's lines were LMS from 1923), through junctions such as Crewe, as troop trains from the Clyde did (p. 116). Lavington was a Great Western station and Porton a Southern Railway one (Wikipedia), so the train changed companies on the way.

Route not in the reports, drawn approximately. By rail from Fort Dix to the Staten Island piers (13 Jan 1943), then convoy UGF-4: out past Sandy Hook on 14 Jan, southeast to a rendezvous, a few hundred miles north of Bermuda on the 16th, east across the Atlantic, British and Canadian escorts joining west of Gibraltar on the morning of the 25th, through the Strait that night, into Mers-el-Kébir on the evening of the 26th. Dates from the Regimental HQ Battery's report and the Ancon's war diary as summarised by the 32nd Station Hospital (32ndstationhospital.com); the mid-ocean track is a guess.

Rail route not in the reports, drawn approximately through the stations of the Oran-Algiers-Constantine main line, in order (Ste-Barbe-du-Tlélat, Perrégaux, Relizane, Inkermann, Orléansville, Duperré, Affreville, El Affroun, Blida, Boufarik, Algiers, Maison-Carrée, Ménerville, Palestro, Bouira, Beni Mansour, Mansourah, Bordj Bou Arreridj, Sétif, Saint-Arnaud, Telergma; placed at today's towns, OSM Nominatim): the line between them isn't traced. Telergma is on the main line; Châteaudun-du-Rhumel isn't. "1 officer and 71 EM boarded the train 2230" at Oran on 10 Feb and arrived at Telergma at 1600 on the 14th, then by truck to Châteaudun; the other 5 officers and 94 men went by motor convoy (rg64-427183820/p0539). The map follows the train party. The train (inferred; the reports say only "train"): the Algerian railways' (CFA) standard-gauge main line from Oran through Algiers to Constantine, single track and steam-hauled, with small engines and hand-braked cars, and slow (Bykofsky and Larson, The Transportation Corps: Operations Overseas, 1957, p. 168). The U.S. Military Railway Service took over CFA lines only from early March 1943, and only east of Beni Mansour (p. 174), so this February train was most likely French-run. Whether the men rode in coaches or in French box cars isn't recorded.
